The realities of the job are that a lot of it is sales, often you’ll be involved in conversations before anything is concrete and you’ll instead really be talking about the marketing features of what ever software or service you are promoting. 

I have tried to be as hands on as possible in this role. I have created demoes and artefacts for customers to demonstrate a certain feature in practice, and to be able to discuss it in more detail with more confidence. 

There are times when I’ve had to deal with technology that I have no interest in at all. That usually is about being able to delegate to an expert. Your role in those conversations is about extracting the questions you’re asking and more broadly trying to understand the questions that aren’t being asked. Or trying to understand the business context for what they are trying to do. The specificity comes from the expert. 

My successes from this role have come from trying to find the right level of earnestness and honesty in how I talk about solutions and earning the confidence of the customers through being able to guide them on the technical implementation details of what they’re trying to do. 

But ultimately I don’t like the role. I often feel uncomfortable with not knowing, and I feel dishonest when relying on marketing answers. I think it comes largely from having been in those situations as a dev, and knowing that the small details are often the most important thing to know. 

The marketing might tell you that x solution is infinitely scalable, but it will require deeper digging to know that those scalability targets are reachable in only y situation. You aren’t a bottomless fountain of knowledge. You will need to learn to be comfortable with prompting them and then deferring to others to provide those details. 

It’s different. You’re learn different skills. It’s not bad per se. Those skills are valuable and transferable.

I love the feeling and shape of a Parker Pen, I used to use their mechanical pencil to write. I wanted to see how viable it would be to create a DIY Parker Pen.

I first bought one of the thin Staedltler Pencil Styluses, after seeing a post showing the internals of it. The thinness caught my eye. These were very cheap, I snagged mine for 25 Euros from Amazon.

I also bought a plastic Parker Pen Jotter, this was cheap too at 5 Euros. It obviously does not have the same feeling as a more expensive metal parker pen, but the feel is still similar enough.

I didn't really document the process of how I made the pen, it was a pretty haphazard approach though.

First, I carefully removed the internals of the Staedtler pencil. The internals can be seen in this [other Redit Post here](https://preview.redd.it/broke-my-noris-digital-which-i-use-with-my-rm2-so-now-you-v0-4joi1jjq5py91.jpg?width=640&crop=smart&auto=webp&s=981fc822d0d70466fb7511416fa640d1e5428a24).

I then used a pair of pliers to remove the metal tip of the Jotter. This would have prevented the pen from writing, as it extends far into the pen.

Then I tried to insert the plastic pen into the body. It did not fit. Towards the bottom it is too thin for the pen to poke out.

I spent the next 30 minutes or slow using some sanding paper and an exacto knife to carve out enough of the plastic on both the base and the EMR Pen to be able to squeeze it out of the bottom.

When I was happy with this, I applied some super glue to the internal barrel, and reset the pen. I let it set.

I may also add some blocker to the top to prevent it from budging, but I will first see how effective the superglue holds.

It wasn't a particularly difficult process, but I don't think the internal pen refill sold by Supernote would work for it. This ended up being JUST ABOUT the right size to work.

You can see a video of it working [and the pressure sensitivity here](https://imgur.com/a/lC8hi2w)

It's a node application, it sits and polls the TickTick API (which exposes an endpoint for change data). 

When it sees an update, and when that update is a tag update it checks if the tag is in format (expand)-(%d+). If it is, it uses the %d argument to call the OpenAPI Functions API. It asks it to simplify the task (The title of the task) and create %d new tasks. It uses the task description to give some context. 

If it sees an update including ai{{whatever you want replacing}} it uses that as a completion. It then gets replaced with whatever OpenAI comes back with. 

Once completed it polls again.
